Why Every Listener try/catches

A throw inside an async listener never reaches emit()'s caller — it becomes an unhandled rejection instead, which is worse, not better.

createTicket calls domainEvents.emit(...) and moves straight on to return ticket — it never awaits anything a listener does, and has no try/catch around the emit() call. That's fine as long as a listener succeeds, but raises a real question: what happens if prisma.notification .createMany(...) above throws — a database hiccup, a constraint violation?

The answer is not "the request fails," even though that might be the instinctive guess. emit() calls each listener but doesn't await an async listener's returned promise — it fires it and returns immediately. A throw inside that async function turns into a rejected promise that nothing is waiting on, which Node reports as an unhandled promise rejection — a background failure with no connection at all back to the request that triggered it, createTicket's return ticket already having happened. The customer's ticket is created either way; the only question is whether that background failure is silently swallowed or actually logged somewhere:

// Figure 5.9: catching inside the listener, not relying on the caller to (src/events/listeners/notifyInApp.listener.js, excerpt)
domainEvents.on(EVENTS.TICKET_ASSIGNED, async (ticket) => {
  try {
    await prisma.notification.create({ /* ... */ });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('notifyInApp listener failed for ticket.assigned:', err);
  }
});

Every listener in all three channel files wraps its body in exactly this shape. It isn't only about turning a silent unhandled rejection into a logged one — with three independent listeners on the same event, a notifyInApp failure that somehow did propagate would still have nowhere useful to propagate to, and (depending on registration order) could stop notifyEmail or notifyRealtime from running for that same event at all. Catching locally, in every listener, is what actually guarantees one channel failing can never take another down with it — the property this whole lesson has been building toward.
